To my elder brother, a genius child, who died.

To my sisters, for whom I gave my entire earning to their marriages.

Meaning

Don’t throw away your failure, your insult, your scrap books, your broken toys, your 8-year gap, your hunger, your bottle diya, your poverty — transform it into your future.

Nothing is waste until you waste it. Transform, don’t throw away.

Part 1 — School Life Foundation p2–100

Chapter 1. St Columbus — Dump Student Tag, Toy Dismantling, No Books, No Chappal, Hunger p2–30

I studied in local St. Columbus School where I was a dump student. All called me “Doctor ka beta kuch nahi janta hai” — Doctor’s son knows nothing.

But truth was different. From childhood I was interested in dismantling my toys and reassembling them again. Combining two parts together to create new multi-purpose toys, like cars — different different cars, modification. One broken car + another broken car = one new car with different functions. That was my first robotics lab at home.

My father is very fond of keeping books. He collects novels, story books and other science and technology books in Hindi, English, and also lots of religion books. He keeps his friend Aneek Kal Singh’s books even after he started his career as a doctor.

I used to collect my sisters’ books — they threw them here and there after exams ended, and I collected them in my almirah rack, two full sections covered with books. Later I started collecting my father’s books also. When I went to a shop and saw a shopkeeper using some books as scrap to put eatables in and give to customers, I usually took those books from him by giving the shopkeeper my old copies and my sister’s old copies.

In St. Columbus, after 3rd class, things improved a little. I got good marks, but due to financial issues we were not allowed to take the marksheet. The teacher and principal then wanted to demote me back to class 2, but my parents came and visited school, and together with my sister’s friend, they insisted the school show if I had actually failed — because in the earlier terminal exam I had failed. My home electricity bill was too much, so they cut the supply lines. So, staying at home without TV, I studied in reality and got good marks. Later, after my parents’ and others’ support, I came to 3rd standard and was not demoted to 2nd standard.

I continued taking average good marks, but the teachers were not satisfied with me. They considered me a dumb student because I didn’t have separate copies for all subjects, couldn’t afford books, and still, for exams, I took my friends’ help and passed — but due to my family’s financial issues we were not able to collect the admit card on time. So I was bullied and scolded by the teacher again.

We had two rooms, and my brother broke the wall so that both rooms could be lit by a single light. We didn’t have electricity because the bill was high and the electricity department had cut our connection, and in the evening we didn’t have much money to even keep our home lit.

During my studies I had no reputation and was just a useless member — I didn’t get new clothes; during festivals my clothes were big-size, rejected clothes bought at half price in the daily market where poor people shop, while my two sisters got new-design, new-style, trendy dresses. My mother used to save to buy them — she hid the money in boxes and saved it from household expenses as my father sent money orders. All our family loans were settled, but we still weren’t able to pay the school fees.

Father went to Bhutan when I started studying, just before my admission to Ashoka Academy. He visited home sometimes, staying more than 15 days — those were the beautiful days of life, when we had enough to eat and got gifts from my father, a jacket and all.

In the family I was like someone no one cared about. My parents’ most-loved and genius child died — my elder brother. My father was always seriously ill and not able to manage household expenses. There was a time, when he was in St. Columbus School, that he didn’t have anything to eat. My elder sister and the middle one and I went in the morning and collected fruits and other eatables so we wouldn’t starve from hunger. Earlier my mother also lay in the hospital, her chances of survival low, having only 3 grams of blood in her body. Relatives from my Nani ghar side came and admitted my mother, and she survived. My mother belongs to a richer family and my father to a poor family, where he suffered the most — he was a villager kisan who did the field work, and with the help of his friends he stood 2nd in Bihar state. His friend Aneek Lal Singh helped him, and he still keeps those books of his even after starting his career as a doctor. My father’s elder brother was a doctor and my grandfather was an LIC officer, but he spent most of his income on all three daughters and his elder son. My father spent his life miserably; he got some money from relatives during his visits, saved it, and bought chocolates and then sold them. In doing so he started his small kirana store business of village origin, to help with the family’s financial issues, because my grandfather was not sending money to the family regularly — he was spending money on the medical studies of his elder son.

My father was once paralyzed and not able to walk. Our home renters, who were mostly truck drivers, helped by massaging his legs and helped him recover a little bit. We had lots of loan credit with the shopkeeper, and the shopkeeper refused to give us any more eatables — then my elder sister, the middle one, and I together went to collect fruits and other vegetables from outside our house. Once, during Hindu–Muslim riots, we had nothing to eat, and then we found ground potatoes growing in our own compound, plenty of them, because there was ‘balu’ in that ground. My father and mother helped the neighbourhood, as there was a complete strike during the Hindu–Muslim riots, and my father distributed the potatoes among the neighbours. This was before my father’s paralysis. My father recovered a little and went to Bhutan and started practicing medicine — he had done his studies through his shop, which he opened with small gifts usually offered in Hindu families. He studied to become a doctor and worked as a local medical practitioner without a degree — it happens in villages, we called it a ‘jholla chaap’ doctor. But he later took his degree from a medical college in Patna and professionally became a doctor and started earning well, and started staying in Darjeeling — that is why he got married into a high-society family. It was an earlier story.

Chapter 2. Nehru Academy — One Year Hindi Medium, and the Inspiration of Captain Vyom p31–40

After 5th class I went to Nehru Academy school and studied one year in Hindi medium. But I had a strong hope to study in a CBSE-based school; my sister heard from her friend and told my mother to shift me to Ashoka Academy school, where English medium was really taught — unlike St. Columbus, which was not much English medium, it was only a rural-level type school.

At Nehru Academy I went all in playing and watching TV serials, and the same at St. Columbus School too. But my favourite serials were Captain Vyom, where time travel and innovation ahead of the future were shown, along with several others shown on national network TV.

Motivation

Captain Vyom inspired me — time travel, future innovation — I thought one day I will make future tech.

Chapter 3. Ashoka Academy — 5th to 6th, the Mixture–Compound Question, Deepchand Valmiki, Bottle Diya, 50% to 89% p41–70

When I went to take admission in Ashoka Academy school, the Director asked me what the difference between a mixture and a compound is. I was speechless. I had spent one year in Hindi medium. Now, about my studies — after 3rd class there was a little improvement at St. Columbus.

I was re-admitted in 5th class because the session was late, and I had to go two months in 5th class before 6th standard. But I was poor at studies; during English class, when the teacher asked me about tense, I didn’t answer, and I took the punishment for that.

Later, one of my area’s boys who studied there, named Deepchand Valmiki, was the child of the cleaning staff who worked in SIRD, Hehal, Ranchi. Though he was poor compared to the other school boys, his family could afford books and copies, unlike mine, which couldn’t even afford chappals to wear — we used to go to the shop barefoot. One day he visited my home with his mother, although he hadn’t talked with me in school before — he came to my house just one week after I joined 5th standard. His mother told me to help him study, as he had been badly beaten within weeks in English class by the teacher, when I got admission to Ashoka Academy and attended the school within weeks — that’s why his mother visited my house.

I was not too bad at studies; I took notes and remembered what the teacher taught me. I didn’t manage separate copies for subjects, but I was a new student in the class, so the teacher hadn’t told me so much about it yet. But they also started shouting at me because I wasn’t able to afford the school uniform.

I taught him his subjects and he went; it became regular, and my studies also stayed on track because he brought books with him. Then, just going into 6th standard, I was not able to come up with money to afford books and copies — my parents hardly managed the uniform, and were unable to pay the fees also.

Then Deepchand Valmiki came with his copy and books and told me to use them, as he was going to Delhi because he had to get his legs operated on, being unable to walk properly. But when he gave me all this, his mother came and started shouting at my mother and me. I returned all his copies and books. Later Deepchand Valmiki came and again gave everything to me, with his mother there — he argued with his mother about it. He became my friend. We didn’t have electricity because the bill was high and the electricity department had cut our connection, and in the evening we didn’t have much money to keep our home lit. Two rooms, and my brother broke the wall so both rooms could be lit by a single light.

My mother went to school to collect the admit card, and the Director told her that if I came with good marks he would reduce the fees to half the original fee of Rs 300 per month at that time. I started studying hard using a bottle-made diya to study at night, and got more than 70 percent. Then my percentage kept increasing, up to 89 percent.

In Ashoka Academy I participated in debates, speech competitions and volleyball, and won medals and trophies there. I used to buy old books, and my father took me to buy old books — we were not able to afford tuition like others did. Once my family tried to afford tuition at a very reduced amount, but couldn’t keep paying, and we had to leave that too within 2 months.

“If you have light inside, even a bottle can become a sun.”— Ashish Kumar
Motivation

You don’t need perfect conditions to shine. You need a reason to shine. The world gives you darkness, you make your own diya. Stop waiting for the perfect setup, the perfect laptop, the perfect lab. Start with what you have.

Chapter 4. NSPC Jamshedpur — Matric 5th Topper (2005), Central Academy Left, 8-Year Gap, Sisters’ Marriage p71–100

Then I had to go outside Ranchi to Jamshedpur, as our school was not affiliated with the CBSE board. We had to purchase the uniform of NSPC school, where my parents’ relatives lived, in Jamshedpur. My Mere Mama, bade wale — he was principal of a cooperative college in Jamshedpur, N.N. Thakur — was given a house by the government to stay there. My mother stayed with me during my matriculation examination. I remained there as a ‘convict,’ not allowed any freedom to go and do anything except study. My uncle used to drop me at the school exam hall.

Matriculation 2005, N.S.P.S., 74%, 5th Topper in School. My relatives, my mother’s sister (my aunt), kept telling everyone that I got a good score because my mama (uncle) worked as principal in the Jamshedpur college, and that he had arranged for my marks to be increased in matriculation like that. During her visits to my home — usually no one stayed at home, they all stayed at Harmu, where that uncle who was the principal stayed. He could afford a good house and good things that we couldn’t afford either. But whenever anyone came to our home, we always helped them with good food, even if he had to take loan credit from the shopkeeper.

After matriculation, and after leaving school at Central Academy, my mother’s sister visited and I went to Kolkata for a month. She used to always bring up the marks in matriculation, because of my uncle. I didn’t say anything, just kept quiet.

Took admission in 10+2 at Central Academy School — left due to financial problems, not due to failure. After an 8-year gap, 2005–2013, due to family responsibilities, I came back. I worked for the family — two sisters’ marriages — my father sold ancestral lands for both sisters’ marriages.

I worked hard at Eureka Forbes and gave my entire savings for my elder sister’s marriage, and did the same for my other sister’s marriage.

Motivation

Family first, then degree. An 8-year gap is not failure, it is responsibility.

Part 2 — The Turning Point: HN Dutta Sir, Roorkee to Punjab KUKA Lab p101–130

During B.Tech at Roorkee Engineering and Management Technology, I met my mentor HN Dutta Sir, who worked in the Antarctica Acoustic Radar R&D Lab — he developed the Acoustic Radar for Antarctica research, a high-level scientist.

I told him about my projects: an AI-based Robotics Car, Home Automation through Bluetooth module and IR Sensor, Speed Control Motor using a sensor-based mechanism, and Safety Protection for Industries. He said, “Your hands work like an engineer, not like a student. Come to Roorkee.” That is how I became part of the Innovation Lab R&D department. At that time HN Dutta Sir was Research Scientist of the R&D lab at Roorkee College of Engineering, Roorkee. He invited me to visit the Roorkee College lab.

I went from Ranchi to Roorkee with my project files — a train journey, the first time going out of Jharkhand for a technical purpose. There I saw advanced industrial robots, advanced embedded labs, IoT labs, which we never had in Ranchi. He taught me industrial automation and REM Tech lab work.

After Roorkee College, I shifted my Engineering B.Tech transfer to Punjab — Gulzar Group of Institutes (GGI Punjab) — because I was much more interested in Robotics. There was the KUKA Lab, Advanced Robotics; Dev Dutta Sir was in charge of the KUKA Lab, and he taught me about robotics and automation.

That KUKA Lab was the place where I learned industrial robotics, quadcopter, drone, smart luggage, and remote-controlled machinery. The Punjab shift changed my life — from a local diploma topper in Ranchi to a B.Tech ECE topper in Punjab, with a 7.16 CGPA and 10 out of 10 SGPA in my final semester, topper of the last semester.

HN Dutta’s words: “Don’t throw away your failure, transform it into a lab.” That line became my company name later — MVA Robotics — Don’t Throw Away Your Past, Transform It Into Your Future.

“Your hands work like an engineer, not like a student.”— HN Dutta Sir
Motivation

One teacher can change your pincode — from Ranchi to Roorkee to Punjab to the world.

6KS Ganga Hospital and Research Centre — Assistant Manager, 2 Years

Case 1 — Ayushman Bharat, Sadar Hospital Inspection, became hero on the first day: Just after my exams ended, I was called to reach the hospital immediately, as an inspection team was arriving that day from Sadar Hospital to inspect Ayushman Bharat status. I hadn’t even done washing my clothes or packed, as the exam had just ended. I was told to come by cab (they would pay) and that laundry would be handled by hospital cleaning staff. Although it was my first time visiting that hospital, I had been building hospital management software with my friends’ startup, IT Login Kashmir, so I had a detailed layout architecture already. When I reached, the Ayushman Bharat inspection team had arrived; I handled it like I had worked there a long time, using the architecture layout to guide the inspection team through all three floors of the KS Ganga building, explaining the beds and equipment on each floor just from the layout on my mobile. Some important documents were missing — without them, they could cancel Ayushman Bharat. I told them I would bring all documents in the proper sequence, asked what was needed, noted everything, while a nervous colleague searched. I told the manager to go look, took nurses and other staff below the manager to follow me, and kept the inspection team engaged. When I returned, I wrote notes in a diary. The inspection team left. I became a hero among the whole hospital staff. The MD arrived, met me, appreciated the work, and asked the Ayushman Bharat technical team to come fix the portal, which was not opening for uploading the required documents. The technical team reached at night; I didn’t sleep the whole night, showing them the required documents to upload, as gathered from the inspection team.

Case 2 — ₹4–5 Crore Tender FIR Save, mind game: The hospital had applied, using a trust not even a year old, to take a ₹4–5 crore tender, showing an annual turnover in crores, and got an FIR from another tendering company falsely claiming the tender had been completed by our Manager and Co-head. The other sections’ head and the MD hadn’t slept for two days; the Manager was communicating with the Co-head on how to handle visiting auditors and government staff alone over the last two days. In the last two days she called and explained, saying the turnover documents were only partial — could we apply back-dated? I said it was not possible. I told her to draft an application for the auditors’ consideration, citing legal issues — that the trust had not been able to fill in the turnover and would do so later — which might save us, since the auditors would disagree with a back-dated annual turnover audit; the draft would only be for demanding time to delay the FIR. I drafted it. When I reached the hospital, I told her I would solve it, not to worry — she said okay casually and went to her room. I spent the night in the office searching the computer network. Then it struck me: the trust was in the name of the Managing Director, and the Managing Director had been filing his annual turnover regularly. Instead of using the newly created trust, add a clause that the newly created trust company’s owner has a turnover in crores and is capable of taking funds for goods and food delivery in the Adivasi school, Khunti area. Instead of attaching the trust company, I told her to draft the tender application in the name of the Managing Director, since he had taken the bid, and add clauses that he is also the owner of the relevant trust company. It was managed well — the Co-head later went with me to the government office, adding and updating documents with the manager and auditors. Task done — saved the hospital from the FIR.

8-Year Gap, Sisters’ Marriage, Ancestral Land Sold — Still Came Back

2005 Matric, 74%, 5th Topper — to 2013 Diploma — an 8-year gap. Father sold ancestral lands for both sisters’ marriages. I was working at Eureka Forbes as a door-to-door salesperson and didn’t spend any money during that period — I had no bank account of my own, so the whole amount stayed with the company. During my leave, I withdrew my entire savings and gave it to my father to support my sister’s marriage; it was a small amount, not enough to save the ancestral land, but some land remained unsold because of it. After her marriage, my other sister was also of marriage age; I didn’t keep my earnings from my job — I worked at the event company Media Sata, starting by sharing templates with students, later taking the whole admission-fair contract, and also worked events for the Reliance Mart Dettol promotion under the same event company, then worked at a job-consultant company at Rospha Tower, Ranchi — and whatever I earned, I gave entirely to my father for my other sister’s marriage, though it still wasn’t enough to save the remaining ancestral land. After both sisters’ marriages, I continued my studies in Diploma EEE.

Behaviour: Family first, then self.

Struggled from barefoot to book collection to Bharat AI.

Extra Chapters

Extra Chapter 1 — The Bottle Diya

Event: No electricity in the mud house in Hehal, Ranchi. Studied — 70% to 89% — by the flame of a plastic-bottle oil diya.

“If you have light inside, even a bottle can become a sun.”— Ashish Kumar
Motivation

You don’t need perfect conditions to shine. You need a reason to shine. The world gives you darkness, you make your own diya. Lesson for the reader: stop waiting for the perfect setup, the perfect laptop, the perfect lab. Start with what you have.

Extra Chapter 2 — Barefoot to Bharat AI + My Books, 2 Almirah Racks Full of Scrap Books

My behaviour with books is different from normal people. Normal students throw books away after exams. I collected.

After exams end, my sisters threw their books here and there — I collected them into an almirah rack, two full sections covered with books. Then I started collecting my father’s books also.

My father is very fond of keeping books — he collects novels, story books, and other science and technology books in Hindi, English, and also lots of religion books. He keeps his friend Aneek Kal Singh’s books even after he started his career as a doctor; he keeps those books even today. I learned my book-collection behaviour from my father.

When I went to a shop and saw a shopkeeper using books as scrap to wrap eatables and give to customers, I used to take those books from him, giving him my old copies and my sister’s old copies in exchange. The shopkeeper thought it was scrap — for me it was gold.

No separate copies for subjects, couldn’t afford books, barefoot to the shop — but still I had 2 almirahs full of books, because I never threw away books. Don’t throw away your past, transform it into your future — my books are proof.

During the 8-year gap, 2005–2013, when I left studies due to financial problems, my books were my university. I read my collected books — science, technology, religion, novels. That’s why, after the 8-year gap, I could become Diploma 2nd Topper with 76.45% — because books never left me, I never left books.

In Diploma, I had no money for new books — used the old books Deepchand Valmiki gave me when he went to Delhi for his leg operation. I returned them when his mother shouted, but he gave them to me again, arguing with his mother. That book gave me knowledge.

At B.Tech, GGI Punjab, I was reading books — Master Class Excel, Embedded, IoT, ML, Data Science, AWS — all from Pantech Solutions. Book learning.

In MCA currently, my Scrap Library — 15 books, ₹350 to ₹6,000, jugaad. Healer, ₹100 vs market ₹899. Circular economy — old books to new robots. 15 scrap books = a ₹6,000-worth lab. This is my book behaviour — transform scrap books into a robot lab.

Motivation

Never throw books. One scrap book can become a ₹6,000 robot kit. One old copy can save your exam.

Last Page — The Behaviour Formula: LOSE

L — Learn from every insult (St Columbus dump tag)

O — Offer your plate when others are hungry (the waiter story)

S — Save every rupee and every scrap book (2 almirahs of books, sisters’ marriage earnings)

E — Engage, even without electricity (the bottle diya, 70% to 89%)

Never-Lose Behaviour = Learn + Offer + Save + Engage.

This is why I never lose in any situation — because I transform every loss into a lab.
